quizName: DMV Practice Test #15 20 Questions • Passing Score 16

questions.question: If you must brake and swerve to avoid a hazard, you should:

options.text: Brake first then swerve, or swerve first then brake.
Brake and swerve at the same time.
Choose to do either brake or swerve.
Only use the front brake and do not swerve.

questions.correctAnswerText: Brake first then swerve, or swerve first then brake.
questions.explanation: Do the actions one at a time, not together. Braking while swerving may cause your motorcycle to fall over.

questions.question: If a dog is chasing your motorcycle, you should:

options.text: Kick the dog away.
Ride next to the dog.
Stop and wait for the dog to lose interest.
Go slow at first, then speed up and leave the dog behind.

questions.correctAnswerText: Go slow at first, then speed up and leave the dog behind.
questions.explanation: Slow down and approach the dog, then speed up to escape. For larger animals, brake and be ready to stop.

questions.question: Your lane position should not:

options.text: Help you see better.
Keep you out of other drivers' blind spots.
Invite other drivers to share your lane.
Give you a way to escape if danger comes.

questions.correctAnswerText: Invite other drivers to share your lane.
questions.explanation: Good lane position should help you see and be seen. It should keep you away from wind blasts, blind spots, and road hazards. Your position should discourage others from sharing your lane and give you an escape route.

questions.question: Since motorcycles are hard to see at night, riders should:

options.text: Ride slower at night.
Honk the horn often while riding at night.
Not ride at night.
Stay right in front of other vehicles so their headlights show you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride slower at night.
questions.explanation: Ride slower at night. Also increase your following distance, use other vehicles' lights to see ahead, use your high beam headlight (unless near other traffic), and be ready to change your lane position.

questions.question: Face shields and goggles:

options.text: Never need to be replaced.
Get scratches and become brittle, so they need regular replacement.
Should break easily in a crash so they do not hurt you.
Should block all air from passing through.

questions.correctAnswerText: Get scratches and become brittle, so they need regular replacement.
questions.explanation: Plastic shields and goggles get scratched and brittle over time. Replace them often to stay safe and comfortable.

questions.question: When crossing angled railroad tracks, the safest way is usually to:

options.text: Go straight ahead in your lane.
Cross at a 45-degree angle.
Cross at a 90-degree angle.
Cross at high speed.

questions.correctAnswerText: Go straight ahead in your lane.
questions.explanation: Go straight in your lane. Turning to hit the tracks at a right angle can be unsafe because it may push you into another lane.

questions.question: When braking on a slippery surface, you should:

options.text: Use both the front and rear brakes.
Press the front brake hard and fast to avoid locking the tire.
Use only the rear brake.
Use only one brake at a time.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use both the front and rear brakes.
questions.explanation: Use both brakes to slow down on slippery surfaces. Squeeze the brake lever slowly and use gentle pressure on the rear brake to avoid locking the front wheel.

questions.question: If a small animal enters your lane while you are in traffic, you should:

options.text: Swerve into other lanes to avoid hitting the animal.
Change lanes quickly.
Stay in your lane.
Flash your lights to scare the animal.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay in your lane.
questions.explanation: Try to avoid hitting an animal safely. In traffic, stay in your lane. Swerving into other traffic to miss a small animal can cause a crash with another vehicle. Hitting a small animal is safer than hitting another car.

questions.question: When riding in a group, less experienced riders should ride:

options.text: Right behind the leader.
In front of the group.
At the back of the group.
Next to the leader.

questions.correctAnswerText: Right behind the leader.
questions.explanation: Less experienced riders should ride toward the front, just behind the leader. This lets experienced riders watch them without making the new rider lead.

questions.question: Because motorcycles are small, they seem to be:

options.text: Going faster than they actually are.
Going slower than they actually are.
Not moving when they are moving.
Closer than they actually are.

questions.correctAnswerText: Going faster than they actually are.
questions.explanation: Because of their small size, motorcycles may look like they are going faster than they really are.

questions.question: What is the best formation for a group of riders going around a curve?

options.text: Pyramid
Staggered
Single-file
Compressed

questions.correctAnswerText: Single-file
questions.explanation: Use single-file formation when going around curves, turning, or entering or exiting a highway. Staggered formation is good for staying close while riding straight.

questions.question: When weight shifts to the front of your bike while braking, you should:

options.text: Gradually increase pressure to the front brake.
Use more rear brake pressure.
Not worry. The weight transfer will not have an effect on your motorcycle.
Try to lock the front tire.

questions.correctAnswerText: Gradually increase pressure to the front brake.
questions.explanation: As your bike's weight moves forward to the front tire during braking, gradually press harder on the front brake lever.

questions.question: Which statement is true?

options.text: The front and rear brakes provide equal braking power.
The front brake provides more braking power than the rear brake.
The rear brake provides more braking power than the front brake.
Only the front brake should be used when braking.

questions.correctAnswerText: The front brake provides more braking power than the rear brake.
questions.explanation: The front brake is more powerful than the rear brake. It provides at least 70 percent of your total stopping power. Always use both brakes when you slow down or stop.

questions.question: When another vehicle is passing you, you should:

options.text: Ride in the left portion of your lane.
Ride in the center portion of your lane.
Ride in the right portion of your lane.
Try to get onto the shoulder.

questions.correctAnswerText: Ride in the center portion of your lane.
questions.explanation: Ride in the center of your lane when being passed. The sides of the lane are less safe because they increase collision risk or may make the other driver return too soon.

questions.question: Riding on the far side of a lane when following another vehicle:

options.text: Is recommended because you will be seen easily.
Is not recommended because drivers seldom use their side mirrors and may not see you.
Is recommended because a passenger in the vehicle may tell the driver that you are there.
Is illegal because you have to ride in the center portion of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Is not recommended because drivers seldom use their side mirrors and may not see you.
questions.explanation: Most drivers look at their rearview mirror more often than their side mirrors. Ride in the center of the lane to be more visible in the driver's rearview mirror.

questions.question: The center portion of a lane:

options.text: Is always the best part of the lane for a motorcycle.
Often contains oil and grease, but is usually safe for riding.
Often contains oil and grease, and is never safe for riding.
Is the smoothest part of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Often contains oil and grease, but is usually safe for riding.
questions.explanation: Oil drippings from cars collect in the center of each lane. On dry roads, this area is usually safe to ride on. Avoid big buildup of oil and grease at busy intersections or toll booths.

questions.question: Under normal conditions, maintain a minimum following distance of:

options.text: One second.
Two seconds.
Three seconds.
Four seconds.

questions.correctAnswerText: Four seconds.
questions.explanation: Keep at least four seconds of distance between your bike and the vehicle ahead in normal conditions. Increase this distance when conditions are worse than normal.

questions.question: A group of riders in staggered formation is passing a car on the left. After the lead rider passes, they should:

options.text: Return to the right portion of their original lane.
Return to the center portion of their original lane.
Return to the left portion of their original lane.
Signal the other riders to follow.

questions.correctAnswerText: Return to the left portion of their original lane.
questions.explanation: After passing, the lead rider should move to the left portion of their lane and maintain passing speed. This opens space for the next rider. Moving to the right portion is unsafe because it may encourage the next rider to pass too soon.

questions.question: The oily strip in the center of a lane:

options.text: Is not safe for motorcyclists at any time.
Is usually safe for motorcyclists, unless it is raining.
Should always be avoided since other parts of the lane do not have the oily strip.
Adds to traction for most motorcycle tires.

questions.correctAnswerText: Is usually safe for motorcyclists, unless it is raining.
questions.explanation: Oil drippings collect in the center of the lane. On dry roads, this area provides enough traction to ride safely. The strip is usually about two feet wide, so you can often ride to one side of it and still be in the center portion of the lane.

questions.question: Studies show that nearly ______ of riders killed in motorcycle crashes had been drinking.

options.text: 20 percent
40 percent
60 percent
80 percent

questions.correctAnswerText: 40 percent
questions.explanation: Alcohol causes many motorcycle crashes, especially fatal ones. About 40 percent of motorcycle riders killed in crashes had been drinking.
